content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses zero-shot visual question answering by leveraging several pretrained models: large language models, image captioning, question generation, and image-text matching. content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- The proposed solution does not require any training, so it can be conducted without large datasets and computation resources.
- The proposed solution exploits frozen models, showing good compatibility between them for the target task.

Weaknesses
- The paper does not propose any model but a very elaborated prompt engineering solution. Whether this solution generalizes well is not clear. For example, is the good performance coming mostly because of the LLM choice? The title and description of the method look like the method is generic to any LLM, but experiments are only conducted on OPT. How well will perform with a different LLM is unclear.
- The dataset choice is somehow concerning. VQAv2 is known to be statistically biased, and OK-VQA and A-OK-VQA require external knowledge to be answered. Given these datasets, how well the proposed solution really interprets and understands the content of the images instead of exploiting the correlations in the language is unclear.
- Ablation on how important the captioning model is missing. Image captioning models are not perfect, so my guess is the choice of the captioning model may have an important impact on the final result. For generalization purposes, it would be better to show the effect when captions are generated with different models.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5P1h
content.comment:
Thank  you for the recognition of the main idea of paper. We provide the response for addressing your concerns, and we sincerely hope that you can reconsider the evaluation. If you have further concerns, please feel free to raise.


1. **How well will perform with a different LLM is unclear.:**

      A: Thanks for your suggestion. Because some classic LLMs, e.g., GPT-3/PaLM/Gother are not available, we only conducted the experiment with some open-sourced LLMs, e.g., GPT-J, GPT-NEO and BLOOM. The results are shown as follows:  

Methods | Shot-Number |  VQAv2 val | OK-VQA |
| ----------- |  ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | 
| PICa 175B | 0 | - | 17.7 |
| Frozen 7B | 0 | 29.5 | 5.9 |
| Ours GPT-NEO 2.7B | 0 | 50.1 | 31.5|
| Ours  OPT 2.7B | 0 | 53.6 | 33.3 |
| Ours  GPT-J 6B | 0 |56.4 |37.4|
|Ours  BLOOM 7.1B | 0 |52.4 | 32.4 |
|Ours  OPT 6.7B | 0 | 57.6 | 38.2|

The experimental results indicate that Img2Prompt enables various LLMs to perform VQA tasks, and that all of them are capable of achieving superior performance to zero-shot PICa and Frozen. This is a strong support for showing our method’s generalization ability with different LLMs. In addition, we find two interesting phenomena 

a) Other open-source LLMs perform marginally worse than OPT. This is due to the fact that other LLMs were trained on smaller datasets than OPT. 

b) The multi-linguistic language model, BLOOM, performs marginally worse than English-specific LLMs.

2.**how well the proposed solution really interprets and understands the content of the images instead of exploiting the correlations in the language is unclear.**

A: Good question. We address your concern from two points:

 (a) Because our method have no access to the training dataset, we cannot learn and leverage the language bias in the training set. This is the advantage of zero-shot vqa.

(b) For the language bias in the large language model itself. We provide the ablation study on OPT30B as follows:
  | Prompts |       OKVQA |
| -----|------|
|question only |   9.5%|
|img2prompt   |  41.8%|

"The question only" prompts use the test question regardless of the image content as prompts, so that LLM can only answer the question according to its language bias. We can see that Img2prompt-generated prompts significantly improve VQA performance (42.0% vs. 9.5%), which is strong evidence that the performance achieved by our method does not rely solely on exploiting correlations in the language.


 3. **how much of this is due to the difference in the image caption generation model?**
     
     A:The LLM’s performance in VQA is impacted by (1) the quality of the image captions and (2) the relevance of the captions w.r.t. the questions. Our paper proposes (1) a filtering method to remove noisy captions, and (2) a question-guided caption generation method to improve the relevance. These proposed methods are analogous to any particular image captioning model. Our paper chooses BLIP as the image captioning model due to its state-of-the-art performance and readily-available open-sourced model. Our system can easily replace BLIP with better image captioning models should they emerge, which we leave as future work, but this does not harm our conclusion, i.e., it is feasible to use frozen LLM to perform zero-shot VQA without training. To avoid the misunderstanding, we have revised our paper, and claim that Img2prompt is based on BLIP.

content.title: Response to Reviewer XNvZ
content.comment:
Thanks for your great research taste and the recognition of our idea, motivation and the experimental results.  We address your concerns as follows:

1.**Integrated with fine-tuned models.**

A:  Thanks for your suggestion. We agree that using our method to fine-tune the model for a specific dataset is a good idea. However, as mentioned in the paper, fine-tuning a large language model needs enormous computational resources, e.g. Flamingo is fine-tuned with over 500k TPUv4 hours, but we lack such a resource. We hope that our research  will inspire further research into fine-tuning large language models for VQA tasks.

2.**Integrated with few-shot models.**	

A:  Thanks for your suggestion.  We incorporate our method into the few-shot method, PICa. Specifically, we follow PICa and perform experiments using 16 similar few-shot samples without ensemble inference. The results show that our method can achieve 47.6% with 66B OPT, and 49.2% with 175B OPT, surpassing 46.5\% achieved by the same setting of PICa 175B. This demonstrates that our Img2Prompt can also improve the performance of few-shot methods.

content.title: Response to Reviewer BBCT
content.comment:
Thanks for the recognition of the motivation of our paper. We address your concerns as follows:

1.**The approach is to filter the captioning of the image, which lacks novelty.**

A: Generating the question-relevant captions is just one technique used in our paper; Our main contribution is, we are the first one to empirically demonstrate that it is feasible to use frozen LLM to perform zero-shot VQA without training. This design can even achieve comparable to or better performance than methods that need few-shot samples or costly end-to-end training, which brings two benefits:

  (a) Reduceing the LLM deployment costs, e.g., Flamingo needs over 500k TPUv4 hours. This is beneficial for small businesses.
  
  (b) It is flexible to use our method with different LLMs, instead of re-finetuning parameters for each new LLM.

2. **In the VQA-v2 official website, it mentioned that "When comparing to the state of the art (e.g., in papers), results should be reported on test-standard. " This paper only reported the test-dev split.**

A: Thanks for pointing it out. As seen in Table 2 of the main paper, the two key zero-shot baselines, VLKD and Flamingo, only publish the VQA score in the test-dev split rather than the test-standard split. Therefore, we also report the VQA score in the test-dev split for a fair comparison. In particular, the VQAv2 test-dev split has over 100,000 samples, which is sufficient to evaluate the performance of VQA models. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves higher performance over these two baselines that require costly end-to-end training. 

3. **Even with a higher computational cost, the performance gap between the proposed model and the pretrained-based model is too large.**

A: As clearly stated in the main paper, we focus on the zero-shot VQA task. In this setting, the model has no access to the training data, and thus has lower scores than those models fine-tuned for the specific training set. It is unfair to compare our results with theirs. 

Compared with the methods you mentioned, our method enjoys the following benefits:

 (a). Except Flamingo, methods you mentioned mostly focus on the image-grounded VQA,  whereas they may perform poorly on tasks requiring external knowledge and reasoning ability, such as OK-VQA and A-OKVQA.  In contrast, our method is motivated by the desire to leverage the knowledge and reasoning ability into LLM without expensive training. Specifically, as demonstrated in Table 7 of the appendix, even without access to training data, our method outperforms fine-tuned pre-trained models on the challenging A-OKVQA dataset. This provides strong support for the application of LLM to VQA tasks. However, if you want to pre-train the model with LLM using the methods you mentioned, the cost is extremely high. This brings the second benefit of our method.

(b).Reducing the enormous cost of deploying LLM into VQA tasks, e.g., Flamingo needs over 500k TPUv4 hours. While our method can use frozen LLM off-the-shelf in zero-shot VQA task, and achieve comparable performance.
   
(c).More flexible.  Because we do not need to training with LLM, it is flexible to use our method with different LLMs. It is meaningful in this rapidly evolving world.

By contrast, even without training, our method can still achieve comparable or better performance than those methods requiring fine-tuneing in the **zero-shot setting**.
    
4. **How to evaluate whether the prompts are informative and correct?**

A: Good question. How to evaluate the quality of prompts is an open question worth exploring, even if for recent NLP papers [1,2]. In our paper, we evaluate the quality of the visual information encoded in the exemplar prompts using the answer hit rate and the answer noise rate. Answer hit rate (AHR) is defined as the proportion of QA pairs containing the ground-truth answer. Answer noise rate (ANR) is defined as the ratio of ground-truth answers to the total number of tokens in the exemplar prompts.  The experimental results demonstrate that improving both the AHR and the ANR can improve the quality of prompts and VQA performance. 	(Please refer to the 3rd paragraph of Section 4.3 and Table 4 of the main paper.)

5.**How to evaluate the performance of the question generation module?**

A: We provide two types of question generation methods. The one is neural-based, the other is templete-based. As Table 3 in the main paper shows, both methods show comparable results.  Specifically, neural-based question generation model is not designed for VQA task, just a simple model from textQA.



[1] Wei, J., Wang, X., Schuurmans, D., Bosma, M., Chi, E., Le, Q., & Zhou, D. (2022). Chain of thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2201.11903.

[2] Wang, X., Wei, J., Schuurmans, D., Le, Q., Chi, E., & Zhou, D. (2022). Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2203.11171.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper considers an alternative approach to fine-tuning for adapting large language models (LLMs) to the visual question answering (VQA) task in a ***zero-shot*** manner.
The paper proposes an approach called Img2Prompt (Figure 1c). Taking an image as input, the main idea is to generate synthetic VQA pairs (exemplar prompts) and question-relevant captions (caption prompts) as prompts to LLMs. Both the captions and the synthetic VQA pairs would provide image signals and synthetic VQA pairs would teach the models how to perform the VQA task.

OPT are used as LLMs: 6.7B, 13B, 30B, 66B, 175B variants. The downstream tasks are VQAv2, OK-VQA, and A-OKVQA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
- Interesting direction on pushing LLMs to do multimodal tasks
- Sound approach

## Weaknesses
- Motivation and validity of the zero-shot setting
- Confounding factors in empirical results when compared to the baseline.
Please see my detailed comments in “Quality” below
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity
The paper is generally clear. Organization could be further improved so that things are presented in order. For example,
- I think OPT should be mentioned earlier in the text and not in the implementation details.
- In Section 3.1, “We generate a number of captions using either an off-the-shelf image captioning network, or the question-relevant caption generation module (§3.3).” is confusing; do the authors actually generate synthetic VQA pairs from ***question-relevant*** captions?

## Quality
- The overall motivation for using LLMs is ok (fine-tuning is computationally expensive and non-modular) but the motivation for the zero-shot setting (vs. the setting in PICa) can be further provided. 
- The approach is sound. Also sound are the submodules for i) synthetically generating VQA pairs from captions and for ii) generating question-relevant captions (via GradCAM for identifying relevant regions and image-text matching for filtering noisy captions).
- While this approach achieves strong zero-shot results in Table 2, there are quite a few confounding factors that should be addressed. First, how much of this is due to the difference in LLMs? Second, how much of this is due to the difference in the image caption generation model?
- The validity of zero-shot is also in question since the training data for models used to generate prompts may overlap with downstream tasks (VQAv2 and OK-VQA are based on COCO).

## Novelty
I think this approach and the setting is different enough from the most related approach PICa, which uses a generated caption and a few training examples from a VQA task as prompts to GPT-3.

content.title: Response to Reviewer GnMz
content.comment:
Thank you for pointing out that our method is sound and that the direction of the research is interesting. We provide a response to your concerns regarding the zero-short setting and confounding factors, and we sincerely hope you will reconsider the evaluation. If you have additional concerns, please to feel free raise them.

1. **Motivation of the zero-shot setting:**

	A: Thanks  for your suggestion, we have added more descriptions to our updated paper. In summary, the motivations of zero-shot setting are:

      (a) Collecting human annotated VQA data is costly.

      (b) The annotated data may introduce a variety of human biases [1,2], which may make the VQA model brittle towards new answer styles and question types. Even if for few-shot method PICa, its performance is sensitive to the selection of few-shot samples, which requests the selected samples are similar to the test sample (e.g. question and image similarity). However, as a practical and open-ended task, the test question in VQA is not always similar to questions in the training set. In this situation, the selection of few-shot samples will degenerate into random selection. As Table 5 in PICa shows,
| Methods | Shot Number | OKVQA |
| ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | 
| PICa_175B w/o selection | 1 | 34.0
| | 4 | 39.7|
| |16 | 43.3 |
| Img2Prompt_66B | 0 | 43.2 |
| Img2Prompt_175B | 0 | 45.6 |

When the test question is not similar to any sample in the training set, the experimental results clearly show that Img2Prompt outperforms PICa with randomly few-shot samples, indicating that Img2Prompt has better generalisation ability than PICa.  This is because Img2Prompt's performance is not dependent on the quality of few-show samples.

2. **Validation of the zero-shot setting:**

      A: The definition of zero-shot VQA is that the models have no access to the VQA annotation. For example, the baselines in our paper, including FewVLM and VL-KD, both fine-tuned their models on COCO, but they all report zero-shot results because they do not utilise the VQA annotation. Our method is valid for the zero-shot VQA according to this definition.


3. **Different LLMs:**

      A: Thanks for your suggestion. Because some classic LLMs, e.g., GPT-3/PaLM/Gother are not available, we only conducted the experiment with some open-sourced LLMs, e.g., GPT-J, GPT-NEO and BLOOM. The results are shown as follows:  

Methods | Shot-Number |  VQAv2 val | OK-VQA |
| ----------- |  ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | 
| PICa 175B | 0 | - | 17.7 |
| Frozen 7B | 0 | 29.5 | 5.9 |
| Ours GPT-NEO 2.7B | 0 | 50.1 | 31.5|
| Ours  OPT 2.7B | 0 | 53.6 | 33.3 |
| Ours  GPT-J 6B | 0 |56.4 |37.4|
|Ours  BLOOM 7.1B | 0 |52.4 | 32.4 |
|Ours  OPT 6.7B | 0 | 57.6 | 38.2|

The experimental results indicate that Img2Prompt enables various LLMs to perform VQA tasks, and that all of them are capable of achieving superior performance to zero-shot PICa and Frozen. This is a strong support for showing our method’s generalization ability with different LLMs. In addition, we find two interesting phenomena 

a) Other open-source LLMs perform marginally worse than OPT. This is due to the fact that other LLMs were trained on smaller datasets than OPT. 

b) The multi-linguistic language model, BLOOM, performs marginally worse than English-specific LLMs.

 4. **how much of this is due to the difference in the image caption generation model?**
     
     A:The LLM’s performance in VQA is impacted by (1) the quality of the image captions and (2) the relevance of the captions w.r.t. the questions. Our paper proposes (1) a filtering method to remove noisy captions, and (2) a question-guided caption generation method to improve the relevance. These proposed methods are analogous to any particular image captioning model. Our paper chooses BLIP as the image captioning model due to its state-of-the-art performance and readily-available open-sourced model. Our system can easily replace BLIP with better image captioning models should they emerge, which we leave as future work, but this does not harm our conclusion, i.e., it is feasible to use frozen LLM to perform zero-shot VQA without training. To avoid the misunderstanding, we have revised our paper, and claim that Img2prompt is based on BLIP.
